content_units: 4-Week Productivity Test at a Glance
For a 6-person team doing mixed marketing + operations work with frequent interruptions, low tolerance for rigid systems, and already-heavy meeting time,   Kanban   is the best method to test first.
It fits this context because it is:
-   Flexible under interruptions
-   Low-overhead to adopt
-   Visible without adding many meetings
-   Better suited to mixed reactive + planned work   than the other two options
Kanban vs Time Blocking vs Weekly Sprint Planning
Method   Fit for interruptions   Setup effort   Meeting overhead   Flexibility   Best use in your context
Kanban     High     Low     Low       High     Best overall for mixed work and constant reprioritization
Time blocking   Low-Medium   Medium   Low   Low-Medium   Useful for individuals, weaker for shared team workflow
Weekly sprint planning   Medium   Medium-High   Medium-High   Medium-Low   Better for predictable project work than interruption-heavy ops
Best choice: Kanban
Option 1:   Kanban     Visual workflow with minimal process burden; handles incoming work well     Best fit for your team
Start board
- Why it works here:
- Lets the team see all work in one place without forcing rigid time boxes
- Absorbs urgent work better than sprint commitments
- Requires fewer meetings than sprint planning
- Feels lighter than calendar-based time blocking
Trade-off alternative
Option 2:   Time blocking     Good for protecting focus time, but weak for collaborative and interrupt-driven work     Good personal habit, weaker team method
Try calendar
- Main issue here:
- Frequent interruptions will break schedules fast
- Team members may resent tightly planned calendars
- Harder to manage shared operational inflow
Structured but heavier option
Option 3:   Weekly sprint planning     Strong for coordinated project delivery, but adds planning discipline and meeting load     Too heavy for this first test
Sprint guide
- Main issue here:
- More ceremony than your team likely wants
- Interruptions can disrupt sprint commitments
- Risks adding process to a team that already spends 9 hours/week in meetings
Lightweight 4-Week Kanban Rollout
Context for this recommendation
I’m assuming you want   one team-wide method  , not separate systems per person, and that success means better flow, less confusion, and no increase in meeting time.
Phase   Goal   Key Tasks   Deliverable
Week 1   Launch a simple board   Create columns: Backlog, This Week, In Progress, Waiting, Done; define task card format; set WIP limit of 2 per person   Live board with visible work
Week 2   Stabilize flow   Add all new work to board first; use one daily 10-minute check-in; track blocked items   Team habit of using board
Week 3   Improve prioritization   Mark urgent work with one tag only; review where work gets stuck; reduce multitasking   Cleaner priorities and fewer half-done tasks
Week 4   Evaluate results   Review throughput, carryover, blockers, and team sentiment; decide keep/tweak/stop   Go-forward decision
Simple operating rules
- One shared board for the whole team
- Keep columns minimal:   Backlog / This Week / In Progress / Waiting / Done
- Limit active work:   no more than 2 active items per person
- New requests go onto the board before someone starts them
- Replace long status meetings with a   10-minute daily flow check
- Use one priority label only:   Urgent   or nothing
Meeting impact
To avoid adding overhead:
- Convert one existing status meeting into the daily 10-minute board review
- Keep one weekly 25-minute review for reprioritization
- Net effect should be   flat or lower meeting time  , not higher
